text: Every hybrid application talks to quantum hardware through a cloud provider's API — there's no on-premise alternative at any real scale today. Knowing the shape of these APIs, and where they genuinely differ, is what the provider-abstraction layer from the last chapter is built around.

Every major provider follows the same basic lifecycle from your code's point of view: submit, poll or subscribe, retrieve. We'll look at where AWS Braket, IBM Quantum, and Azure Quantum genuinely differ, and why checking device status first is a free call that can save you an expensive one.

Here's that status check in a real console — Amazon Braket's device list. Braket charges a flat per-task fee plus a per-shot fee that varies by hardware vendor. A device flagged offline will reject your submission outright; one with a long queue might make a different device the better choice entirely.

Azure Quantum takes a different shape: a marketplace model where billing terms are set per hardware partner. Here's a real job list from the Azure portal — ID, target, status, submission time, and a cost estimate, all visible before you ever retrieve a result.

And IBM Quantum is different again — billed by wall-clock runtime second, not shot count directly. A circuit shaped like this one determines exactly how long that billable runtime actually is. Three providers, three pricing dimensions — which is exactly why your abstraction layer's cost-estimation method can't be one shared formula.
Next lesson puts the submit-poll-retrieve lifecycle to work for real — measuring, in actual milliseconds, where the time in one hybrid iteration really goes.
